\chapter{The First Verbs}
\label{ch:first-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what language I speak, where I live and what I do, building each sentence from a verb stem, a gender ending and the copula.}

Complete separate oral listening and speaking checks: hear a present-habitual sentence and say what its ending reveals about the speaker, then build three sentences about yourself — your language, your city and your work. Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing remain blocked until \#13068 teaches the forms.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bolṇā]{\pa{ਬੋਲਣਾ} (bolṇā) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} your first full verb}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-bolna}



\begin{quote}
Until now, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{does} something — in a shape you'll see on every Punjabi verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਬ}} (\emph{ba}) + \textbf{\pa{ੋ}} (the \emph{horā}, \emph{o}-sign) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਬੋ}} (\emph{bo}); \textbf{\pa{ਲ}} (\emph{la}); \textbf{\pa{ਣਾ}} (\emph{ṇā}, retroflex \emph{ṇ} + long \emph{ā}). Read \textbf{\pa{ਬੋ}·\pa{ਲ}·\pa{ਣਾ}} $\to$ \emph{bolṇā}.

None of these pieces is yours to read yet. A later session in this chapter teaches \textbf{\pa{ਬ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਲ}} and \textbf{\pa{ੋ}}; until then the word travels by ear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲਣਾ}} (\emph{bolṇā}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is a native Indo-Aryan verb (the same word as Hindi \emph{bolnā}). Its ending \textbf{-\pa{ਣਾ}} (\emph{-ṇā}) is the point: \textbf{every} Punjabi verb, named in the dictionary, ends in \emph{-ṇā} (or \emph{-nā}) — Punjabi's \textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{}: \emph{bol-ṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{mil-ṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{milāṁge}), \emph{rakh-ṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to keep\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{rabb rākhā}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + ending}]
Strip the \emph{-ṇā} and you have the \textbf{stem}: \emph{bol-}. The stem holds the action; endings pin down who and when: \emph{bol-dā} (speaking, m.), \emph{bol-dī} (speaking, f.), \emph{bol} (speak!, familiar command). Every tense in this book is built by adding to a stem like this.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bolṇā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the stem left when you strip \emph{-ṇā} (\emph{bol-})
  \item three verbs whose stems you can now hear (\emph{bol-, mil-, rakh-})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{bolṇā}'s stem, and what do you take off to find it? (\emph{bol-}; the infinitive ending \emph{-ṇā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[panjābī]{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ} (panjābī) — the language names itself after five rivers}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-panjabi}



\begin{quote}
You have a verb for speaking. Before you can say what you speak, you need the name of the language itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਪੰ}} (\emph{paṁ}, with the \emph{ṭippī} nasal) + \textbf{\pa{ਜਾ}} (\emph{jā}) + \textbf{\pa{ਬੀ}} (\emph{bī}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}} (\emph{panjābī}).

Shapes to notice only. Say the word; the reading comes later.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}} (\emph{panjābī}) is the name of the language — and it is \textbf{Persian}: \emph{panj} (\textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{āb} (\textquotedblleft{}water, river\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}the language{]} of the five rivers},\textquotedblright{} for the five great rivers that cross the Punjab. The very name of the language is a small Persian geography lesson.

And \emph{panj} itself is an old relative: it is a distant cousin of English \textbf{five}, Latin \emph{quinque} and Greek \emph{pente}, all from one Indo-European word for the number. A later chapter comes back to \emph{panj} as an ordinary number you can count with.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}panjābī\textquotedblright{}
  \item its two Persian halves (\emph{panj} \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āb} \textquotedblleft{}water, river\textquotedblright{})
  \item the English cousin of \emph{panj} (\emph{five})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Unpack the name \emph{panjābī}, and name the English cousin of its first half. (\emph{Panj} \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āb} \textquotedblleft{}river\textquotedblright{}; \emph{panj} is cousin to English \emph{five}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maiṁ panjābī boldā hāṁ]{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ} \pa{ਬੋਲਦਾ} \pa{ਹਾਂ} (maiṁ panjābī boldā hāṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Punjabi\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-main-punjabi-bolda-han}



\begin{quote}
Three words you already own — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the language, the verb. Here they become your first complete, moving sentence.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ} \pa{ਬੋਲਦਾ} \pa{ਹਾਂ}} = \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ}} (\emph{maiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ}} (\emph{panjābī}, the object) + \textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲਦਾ}} (\emph{boldā}, \textquotedblleft{}speak,\textquotedblright{} m.) + \textbf{\pa{ਹਾਂ}} (\emph{hāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I Punjabi speaking am},\textquotedblright{} with the verb-frame last, exactly as \emph{hai} first showed you.

\textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲਦਾ}} (\emph{boldā}) is the stem \emph{bol-} plus \textbf{-\pa{ਦਾ}} (\emph{-dā}). Nothing new has been added to the verb but an ending.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the present habitual, gendered}]
To say \textquotedblleft{}I do X,\textquotedblright{} Punjabi uses \textbf{stem + -dā/-dī + the copula}, and the participle \textbf{agrees with the speaker's gender}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a man: \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ} \pa{ਬੋਲਦਾ} \pa{ਹਾਂ}} (\emph{boldā hāṁ})
  \item a woman: \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਪੰਜਾਬੀ} \pa{ਬੋਲਦੀ} \pa{ਹਾਂ}} (\emph{boldī hāṁ})
\end{itemize}

The \emph{-dā/-dī} marks the speaker — a feature English has no trace of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ panjābī boldā hāṁ} (a man)  ·  \emph{maiṁ panjābī boldī hāṁ} (a woman)
  \item which ending would be yours (\emph{-dā} or \emph{-dī})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Build \textquotedblleft{}I speak Punjabi\textquotedblright{} as a woman, and say which word changed. (\emph{Maiṁ panjābī boldī hāṁ} — the participle, \emph{boldā} becoming \emph{boldī}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rahiṇā]{\pa{ਰਹਿਣਾ} (rahiṇā) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-rahna}



\begin{quote}
A second verb, so you can say where you live — and watch the \emph{stem + ending} machine work a second time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਰ}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\pa{ਹਿ}} (\emph{hi}) + \textbf{\pa{ਣਾ}} (\emph{ṇā}, the retroflex infinitive) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਰਹਿਣਾ}} (\emph{rahiṇā}). The opening \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} is one you read already.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਰਹਿਣਾ}} (\emph{rahiṇā}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, to remain, to stay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \emph{rah-} (\textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}) — the same verb as Hindi \emph{rahnā}. It covers both \textquotedblleft{}reside\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}keep on\textquotedblright{}: \emph{maiṁ Amritsar rahindā hāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}I live in Amritsar\textquotedblright{}). Stem \emph{rahi-} + \emph{-dā/-dī} + copula, exactly like \emph{bolṇā}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes after the noun (or is dropped)}]
\emph{maiṁ Amritsar rahindā hāṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Amritsar.\textquotedblright{} Punjabi, like Hindi, uses \textbf{post}positions (\emph{vic}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}) where English uses prepositions — and with a place-name it often drops \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} entirely. The verb, as ever, is last.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ Amritsar rahindā hāṁ} (a man)  ·  \emph{maiṁ Amritsar rahindī hāṁ} (a woman)
  \item where Punjabi puts \textquotedblleft{}in,\textquotedblright{} if it says it at all (after the noun)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I live in Amritsar,\textquotedblright{} and name the root of \emph{rahiṇā}. (\emph{Maiṁ Amritsar rahindā/rahindī hāṁ}; Sanskrit \emph{rah-}, \textquotedblleft{}to remain.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karnā]{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ} (karnā) — \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} the verb whose root you met in your first greeting}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-karna}



\begin{quote}
The third verb of the chapter — and the one whose root has been sitting inside a word you have said since your very first greeting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਕ}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\pa{ਨਾ}} (\emph{nā}) $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} (\emph{karnā}). Two of the three pieces are already yours to read.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} (\emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}) is from the Sanskrit root \emph{√kṛ} (\textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-} — one of Sanskrit's most productive roots. You met its family in Chapter 1's \textbf{\pa{ਨਮਸਤੇ}}/\textbf{\pa{ਨਮਸਕਾਰ}} (\emph{namaskār} = \emph{namas} + \emph{kār}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{making} of a bow\textquotedblright{}) and in \emph{karma} (\textquotedblleft{}a thing \textbf{done}\textquotedblright{}). Strip \emph{-nā} and the stem is \emph{kar-}, exactly as \emph{bol-} and \emph{rahi-} came out of their infinitives.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}karnā\textquotedblright{} and its stem (\emph{kar-})
  \item the Chapter-1 word that shares its root (\emph{namaskār} — the \textquotedblleft{}making\textquotedblright{} of a bow)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit root is \emph{karnā} from, and name a Chapter-1 word built on it. (\emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}; \emph{namaskār} — \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kamm karnā]{\pa{ਕੰਮ} \pa{ਕਰਨਾ} (kamm karnā) — \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-kamm-karna}



\begin{quote}
You have \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{} Put a noun in front of it and Punjabi builds a whole family of verbs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੰਮ}} (\emph{kamm}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{\pa{ਕੰ}} (\emph{kaṁ}, with the \emph{ṭippī} nasal) + \textbf{\pa{ਮ}} (\emph{ma}). Both \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਮ}} are already yours.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੰਮ}} (\emph{kamm}) is the noun \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} — the thing done, from the same \emph{√kṛ} family as \emph{karnā}. Said on its own it means a job, a task, a piece of business: \emph{bahut kamm hai} (\textquotedblleft{}there is a lot of work\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: noun + \pa{ਕਰਨਾ}}]
Like Hindi, Punjabi builds countless verbs as \textbf{noun + \pa{ਕਰਨਾ}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕੰਮ} \pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} (\emph{kamm karnā}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to work}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{gall karnā} = \textquotedblleft{}to have a chat\textquotedblright{} (\emph{gall}, the \textquotedblleft{}matter/talk\textquotedblright{} you already know from \emph{koī gall nahīṁ})
\end{itemize}

So \emph{maiṁ kamm kardā hāṁ} = \textquotedblleft{}I work.\textquotedblright{} Learn \emph{karnā} and a whole grammar of \textquotedblleft{}do-verbs\textquotedblright{} opens up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kamm karnā\textquotedblright{} (to work)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) — \emph{maiṁ kamm kardā hāṁ / kardī hāṁ}
  \item one more noun-plus-\emph{karnā} verb (\emph{gall karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to have a chat\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Punjabi say \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} and what is the pattern? (\emph{Kamm karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{}; a noun in front of \emph{karnā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ba · la · -o]{\pa{ਬ} · \pa{ਲ} · \pa{ੋ} — three pieces met inside a word you already say}

\label{lesson:PA-S05-babba-lalla-hora}



\begin{quote}
The stem of this chapter's first verb is three pieces, and they are today's three.

First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tusī̃ kivēṁ ho — maiṁ ṭhīk hāṁ — koī gall nahīṁ} · \emph{rabb rākhā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \pa{ਬ} · \pa{ਲ} · \pa{ੋ}}
\begin{quote}
\pa{ਬ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{babbā} — \emph{ba}. A consonant, the voiced \emph{b} of \emph{bat}, with no breath after it.

\begin{quote}
\pa{ਲ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{lallā} — \emph{la}. A consonant, a clear \emph{l} made at the teeth — never the dark \emph{l} at the end of English \emph{full}.

\begin{quote}
\pa{ੋ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{horā} — \emph{-o}. A mātrā for \emph{o}, written as a single stroke \textbf{above} the head-line.

Now put them where you have already heard them:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਬ}} + \textbf{\pa{ੋ}} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਬੋ}} (\emph{bo});  \textbf{\pa{ਬੋ}} + \textbf{\pa{ਲ}} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲ}} (\emph{bol})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲ}} — \emph{bol} — \textbf{speak — the bare stem of this chapter's first verb}
\end{quote}

You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to \textbf{recognise} it the next time it goes past.

\subsection*{Writing: copy what you can see}
Keep \pa{ਬ} · \pa{ਲ} · \pa{ੋ} in front of you and do not cover any of them. Follow each shape once with a finger, then copy it once with a pencil, larger than it is printed. Say its sound as your hand stops.

\begin{quote}
This is \textbf{observe-and-trace with the model visible}. Nothing in these chapters asks you to write a Punjabi word from memory; that ladder starts later, and it starts from these same shapes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲ}} and point to each of today's pieces in turn
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ba}, \emph{la}, \emph{-o}, then the whole word — \emph{bol}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at the headword at the top of any earlier lesson in this chapter and find one shape you now know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name today's pieces: \emph{babbā}, \emph{lallā}, \emph{horā}. Which of them is a \textbf{mātrā} or a mark rather than a letter, and what does \textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲ}} say? (\emph{bol}, “speak — the bare stem of this chapter's first verb”.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A00.pdf}{Unicode Gurmukhi chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:PA-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one engine — build real sentences about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — three sentences about yourself}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Punjabi\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) — \emph{maiṁ panjābī boldā/boldī hāṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Amritsar\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ Amritsar rahindā/rahindī hāṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ kamm kardā/kardī hāṁ}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the engine}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} what you strip off an infinitive to reach the stem (\emph{-ṇā}/\emph{-nā})
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two agreements in a present sentence (\emph{-dā/-dī} for gender; \emph{hāṁ/haiṁ/ho} for person)
  \item \emph{Say it:} where the verb sits, and which side of a noun \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} would sit (last; after the noun)
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\pa{ਬੋਲ}} and name this chapter's three pieces — \emph{babbā}, \emph{lallā}, \emph{horā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bolṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (native Indo-Aryan)
  \item \emph{rahiṇā} \textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{karnā} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{√kṛ} — the root of \emph{namaskār} and \emph{karma}
  \item \emph{panjābī} $\leftarrow$ \emph{panj} \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} (cousin of English \emph{five}) + \emph{āb} \textquotedblleft{}river\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, tell me your language, your city, and your work in Punjabi (as a woman). (\emph{Maiṁ panjābī boldī hāṁ. Maiṁ … rahindī hāṁ. Maiṁ kamm kardī hāṁ.})

Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing are \textbf{not scored here}. Romanization is evidence for spoken recall only; a typed romanization never counts as Gurmukhi writing.
\end{tcolorbox}
